01.note: Three Sages, Rav Pappa, Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua and Rava bar Shmuel, ate bread together, and each claimed the honor of leading Grace after Meals. Rav Pappa said he should lead because he had poured nine kav of water over himself. Rava bar Shmuel answered that nine kav suffices only for oneself, while one who acts for others needs forty se'a, and he had immersed in forty se'a. Rav Huna said he should lead, since he had needed neither, having remained pure.
01.why: The discussion turns on how much water restores purity: nine kav poured over a person or forty se'a, and whether the vessel matters. The meal plays out those levels, and the Gemara then rules against distinguishing purity for oneself from purity for others.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: Claims to lead Grace because nine kav of water fell on him.

people.name: Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua
people.about: Claims to lead because he needed no purification at all.

people.name: Rava bar Shmuel
people.about: Claims to lead because he immersed in forty se'a.

terms.meaning: The blessings said after eating bread; one person can lead and recite them on behalf of the whole group.
Measures of volume. Nine kav is a modest amount of water poured over the body; forty se'a is the volume of a ritual bath (mikveh) for full immersion.

02.note: A student going into a bathroom left his phylacteries in a hole in the wall facing the public street. A prostitute passing by took them, came to the study hall and said: See what so-and-so gave me as my payment. When the student heard this, he went up to the roof, fell and died. At that time the Sages instituted that a person should hold his phylacteries in his hand, covered with his garment, when he goes in.
02.why: A teaching had just warned against leaving phylacteries in holes facing the public domain, lest passersby take them and the owner fall under suspicion; this incident is the reason behind that warning and the rule that replaced it.

people.name: a student
people.about: Left his phylacteries in a wall hole facing the street; was falsely shamed and died.

people.name: a prostitute
people.about: Took the phylacteries and displayed them in the study hall as payment.

terms.meaning: Tefillin: small leather boxes holding Torah passages, worn on the arm and head; they may not be brought into a bathroom carelessly.
The house of study where the Sages and their students learned Torah.

03.note: Rabba bar bar Ḥana recalled walking behind his teacher Rabbi Yoḥanan: when Rabbi Yoḥanan went into a bathroom holding a book of aggada, he would hand it to his students, but phylacteries he kept, saying: Since the Sages permitted holding them, they will protect me. Rava told the same of Rabbi Naḥman: the book he handed over, the phylacteries he kept, with the same words.
03.why: The Gemara has been setting out how phylacteries are carried when not worn, rolled in the hand by day or in a pouch by night. These reports show two Sages choosing to keep them in hand, as permitted, rather than give them to someone else.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Ḥana
people.about: Reports what he saw while walking after Rabbi Yoḥanan.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: Gave his students his book of aggada but kept his phylacteries.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Reports the same conduct of Rabbi Naḥman.

people.name: Rabbi Naḥman
people.about: Kept his phylacteries in hand, saying they would protect him.

terms.meaning: The non-legal teachings of the Sages: stories, sayings and interpretations of Scripture.
Tefillin: leather boxes holding Torah passages, worn on arm and head during prayer and study.

04.note: Rav Hamnuna, son of Rav Yosef, recalled standing before Rava, who told him to go and bring his phylacteries. He found them in Rava's bed, between the mattress and the pillow, not directly under where his head lay. Rav Hamnuna knew it was the day of Rava's wife's immersion, and understood that Rava had sent him for them to teach the practical law.
04.why: Rabbi Yirmeya had just ruled that phylacteries kept under one's head at night belong between the pillow and the mattress, off to the side of the head; this incident shows Rava following that ruling in practice.

people.name: Rav Hamnuna, son of Rav Yosef
people.about: Was sent by Rava to fetch his phylacteries and tells what he found.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Kept his phylacteries in his bed and sent his student for them to teach the law.

terms.meaning: Tefillin: leather boxes holding Torah passages, worn on arm and head.
The day a wife immerses in a ritual bath after menstruation, after which marital relations are permitted again.

05.note: Rabbi Abba wanted to move to the Land of Israel and was avoiding his teacher Rav Yehuda, who held that anyone who leaves Babylonia for the Land of Israel transgresses a commandment, citing Jeremiah. Before leaving, he decided to go hear one more teaching at the Sages' assembly. There he heard a teaching on a man who passes wind while praying: he steps back four cubits, waits for the odor to pass, says a short prayer confessing that God made us full of openings, and resumes where he stopped. Rabbi Abba said: Had I come only to hear this, it would have been enough.
05.why: The Gemara has just distinguished sneezing from above, a good sign in prayer, from sneezing from below, passing wind; this story brings the teaching on what one does after passing wind in the middle of prayer.

people.name: Rabbi Abba
people.about: Student of Rav Yehuda who wanted to move to the Land of Israel.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: Rabbi Abba's teacher, who held that leaving Babylonia for the Land of Israel is a transgression.

terms.meaning: Here, a man whose job was to recite memorized teachings aloud before the Sages.
The Land of Israel.
About two meters; a standard distance in Jewish law.

06.note: Rav Aḥai arranged for his son to marry into the family of Rav Yitzḥak bar Shmuel bar Marta. He brought his son into the wedding canopy, but the son could not consummate the marriage. Rav Aḥai went in after him to look into it and saw a Torah scroll lying there. He said to them: Had I not come now, you would have endangered my son's life. He cited a teaching that relations are forbidden in a room with a Torah scroll or phylacteries unless they are taken out or put in a vessel inside a second vessel.
06.why: The Gemara is discussing what must screen or separate holy objects and bodily matters; this story introduces the rule about a Torah scroll in a bedroom, which Abaye, Rava and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi go on to refine.

people.name: Rav Aḥai
people.about: Father of the groom; found the Torah scroll in the bridal room.

people.name: Rav Yitzḥak bar Shmuel bar Marta
people.about: The family his son married into.

terms.meaning: The huppah, here the chamber where the couple first came together.
A double covering, such as a box within a box, which counts as removing a holy object from the room.
Tefillin: leather boxes holding Torah passages, worn on arm and head.

07.note: Mar Zutra visited Rav Ashi's house and saw a Torah scroll in the bedroom of Rav Ashi's son, Mar bar Rav Ashi, with a partition ten handbreadths high set up around it. He asked whose opinion they were following. If Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's, he said, that applies only to someone who has no other room; the Master has another room. Rav Ashi's answer was: It did not occur to me.
07.why: The Gemara is listing ways to screen a Torah scroll in a room used for marital relations, including Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's ten-handbreadth partition; the story limits that partition to someone with no other room.

people.name: Mar Zutra
people.about: Visitor who questioned the partition.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: Host; admitted the other room had not occurred to him.

people.name: Mar bar Rav Ashi
people.about: Rav Ashi's son, in whose bedroom the Torah scroll stood.

terms.meaning: A measure of about 8 to 10 centimeters; ten handbreadths is the standard height of a partition that counts as a separate space.

07.flag: The story segment opens mid-sentence with the end of Rava's ruling and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's statement before the Mar Zutra incident begins.

08.note: Rav visited the house of Geniva and recited the Shabbat evening prayer on Friday while it was still day. Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba was praying behind him. Rav finished his prayer but did not step back, so as not to interrupt Rabbi Yirmeya's prayer. The Gemara draws three rulings from this: one may pray the Shabbat prayer before Shabbat begins, a student may pray behind his teacher, and one may not pass in front of people who are praying.
08.why: The Gemara is asking whether the afternoon prayer ends at midafternoon, as Rabbi Yehuda holds, and has just pointed to Rav praying the Shabbat prayer early; it then questions how Rabbi Yirmeya could pray behind his teacher at all.

people.name: Rav
people.about: Prayed the Shabbat prayer early at Geniva's house.

people.name: Geniva
people.about: The Sage whose house Rav visited.

people.name: Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba
people.about: Was praying behind Rav.

terms.meaning: Friday before nightfall, when Shabbat begins.
At the end of the Amida prayer one takes three steps back; doing so here would have meant passing in front of Rabbi Yirmeya.

09.note: Avidan reported that once the sky became so overcast that the people thought night had fallen. They went into the synagogue and recited the evening prayer for the end of Shabbat while it was still Shabbat. Then the clouds cleared and the sun shone. They came and asked Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi what to do, and he said: Since they have prayed, they have prayed.
09.why: The Gemara asked whether a prayer said by mistake can be undone; Avidan's report suggests it cannot, and the Gemara answers that a community is different, since it is not burdened with praying again.

people.name: Avidan
people.about: Reports the incident.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who ruled that the prayer stood.

terms.term: prayer of the conclusion of Shabbat
terms.meaning: The evening prayer said as Shabbat ends, which marks the passage from Shabbat to the weekday.

10.note: A student asked Rabbi Yehoshua whether the evening prayer is optional or obligatory; he said optional. Rabban Gamliel said obligatory, raised the question before the assembled Sages, made Rabbi Yehoshua stand to admit his view, and left him standing while he lectured. The angry assembly removed Rabban Gamliel and appointed the eighteen-year-old Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, whose hair miraculously turned white. That day the study hall was opened to all students, and Rabbi Yehoshua's view prevailed over Rabban Gamliel's on an Ammonite convert. Rabban Gamliel went to apologize, found Rabbi Yehoshua's walls black from smithing, was rebuked, and was forgiven for his father's sake. Rabbi Yehoshua then urged his return, and Rabbi Akiva agreed to go to Rabban Gamliel's door the next morning.
10.why: The mishna says the evening prayer is not fixed, which the Gemara reads as the view that it is optional, the dispute between Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Yehoshua. This is how that dispute unfolded.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: Ruled the evening prayer optional; was humiliated by Rabban Gamliel and later forgave him.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: Head of the Sages (the Nasi); ruled the prayer obligatory and was removed from office.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya
people.about: Chosen to replace Rabban Gamliel; wise, rich and descended from Ezra.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Considered for the post; later had the gates locked, then agreed to go to Rabban Gamliel.

people.name: Yehuda, the Ammonite convert
people.about: Asked whether he could marry into the Jewish people.

terms.meaning: The head of the Sages and the leader of the Jewish community.
The Gemara's name for the Torah scholars who do battle in the study of Torah.
The man who repeated the lecturer's words aloud to the assembly; when he stopped, the lecture stopped.
Marry a Jewish woman; the Torah bars Ammonites from doing so.

11.note: When Rabbi Eliezer fell ill, his students came to visit him and asked him to teach them paths of life by which they would earn the World-to-Come. He told them: Be careful of your colleagues' honor; keep your children from logic; seat them, while young, at the knees of Torah scholars; and when you pray, know before Whom you stand. For this, he said, you will earn the World-to-Come.
11.why: It follows Rabbi Neḥunya ben Hakana's prayers on entering and leaving the study hall, opening a run of related deathbed teachings; its last instruction, to know before Whom one stands in prayer, bears on the chapter's subject of prayer.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: Sage who, when ill, gave his students guidance for life.

terms.meaning: The life after this one, in which the righteous are rewarded.
The translation explains this as keeping them from reasoning about verses in ways that lead to heresy.

12.note: When Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Zakkai fell ill, his students visited him, and he began to cry. They asked why. He said that before a human king, whose anger, prison and killing are not forever and who can be appeased or bribed, he would still cry; now he was being led before the King of Kings, whose anger, prison and killing are forever, with two paths before him, to the Garden of Eden or to Gehenna, not knowing which. Asked to bless them, he wished that their fear of Heaven be like their fear of people, since a sinner says: I hope no one sees me. As he died he told them to clear out the vessels because of impurity, and to prepare a chair for Hezekiah, King of Judea, who was coming.
12.why: The Gemara sets it beside the account of the students visiting Rabbi Eliezer, Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Zakkai's student, on his sickbed, so the teacher's parting words follow the student's.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Zakkai
people.about: Rabbi Eliezer's teacher; wept on his sickbed in fear of divine judgment.

people.name: Hezekiah, the King of Judea
people.about: The biblical king whom Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Zakkai said was coming as he died.

terms.meaning: The place of punishment after death; the Garden of Eden is the place of reward.

terms.term: remove the vessels due to impurity
terms.meaning: A dead body makes everything under the same roof ritually impure, so household items were taken out beforehand.

13.note: In Yavne, Shimon HaPakuli set the eighteen blessings of the daily prayer in order before Rabban Gamliel. Rabban Gamliel asked the Sages whether anyone knew how to compose a blessing against the heretics, and Shmuel HaKatan stood up and composed it. The next year, leading the prayer, Shmuel HaKatan forgot that blessing and tried for two or three hours to recall it, and they did not remove him from leading the prayer.
13.why: The Gemara asked why the eighteen blessings are nineteen, and Rabbi Levi said the blessing against heretics was added at Yavne; this tells how. The Gemara then asks why Shmuel HaKatan was not removed, given Rav's rule that one who errs in that blessing is removed as a suspected heretic.

people.name: Shimon HaPakuli
people.about: Set the eighteen blessings in order before Rabban Gamliel.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: Asked who could compose the blessing against the heretics.

people.name: Shmuel HaKatan
people.about: Composed the blessing, then forgot it a year later.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Argues in the Gemara that a good person does not become wicked.

people.name: Yoḥanan the High Priest
people.about: Cited as one who served eighty years and became a Sadducee.

terms.meaning: The Amida, the central standing prayer said each day.
A blessing added to the Amida asking God to bring down heretics and informers.
The person who recites the prayer aloud for the congregation.
A member of a Second Temple group that rejected the Sages' teachings.

13.flag: The story segments run on into the Gemara's question-and-answer about why Shmuel HaKatan was not removed and stop mid-argument, before the answer that closes it.

14.note: The Gemara cites a mishna: Do not be sure of yourself until the day you die, for Yoḥanan the High Priest served in the High Priesthood for eighty years and in the end became a Sadducee.
14.why: Abaye had said that one who is righteous from the start never turns wicked, to explain why Shmuel HaKatan was not suspected of heresy; the Gemara cites Yoḥanan the High Priest to challenge him.

people.name: Yoḥanan the High Priest
people.about: Served as High Priest for eighty years and finally became a Sadducee.

terms.meaning: A member of a Second Temple group that rejected the Sages' teachings.
The chief priest who served in the Temple in Jerusalem.

14.flag: A single sentence quoted as a counter-example in the middle of an argument; it overlaps the end of the Shmuel HaKatan story and has almost no narrative of its own.

15.note: Rav Ḥisda and Rav Sheshet were walking along the road when Rav Ḥisda stopped, stood and recited the traveler's prayer. Rav Sheshet, who could not see, asked his servant what Rav Ḥisda was doing, and was told he was standing and praying. Rav Sheshet said: Stand me up too, and I will pray. From being good, do not be called wicked.
15.why: Rav Ḥisda had ruled that the traveler's prayer is said standing, and Rav Sheshet that it may be said walking; here Rav Sheshet stands anyway, showing that his ruling permitted walking but did not prefer it.

people.name: Rav Ḥisda
people.about: Stopped on the road to say the traveler's prayer standing.

people.name: Rav Sheshet
people.about: Blind Sage who asked his servant to stand him up to pray as well.

terms.meaning: A short prayer for a safe journey, said when setting out on the road.

16.note: Abaye was sitting before his teacher Rabba, and Rabba saw that he was very merry. Rabba said: It is written, Rejoice with trembling. Abaye answered: I am wearing phylacteries.
16.why: Rabba had just taught that the verse rejoice with trembling means that even in rejoicing there should be trembling; here he applies it to his student, who answers that his phylacteries keep him in awe.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Rabba's student, rebuked for being too merry.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: Abaye's teacher, who quoted the verse to him.

terms.meaning: Tefillin: leather boxes holding Torah passages, worn on arm and head; the translation explains that wearing them keeps the fear of God on a person.

17.note: Rabbi Yirmeya was sitting before Rabbi Zeira, who saw that he was very merry. Rabbi Zeira said to him: It is written, In all sorrow there is profit. Rabbi Yirmeya answered: I am wearing phylacteries.
17.why: It is the second of a run of stories about holding excessive joy in check, after Rabba's rebuke of Abaye with the verse rejoice with trembling; the reply is the same.

people.name: Rabbi Yirmeya
people.about: Was very merry and answered that he was wearing phylacteries.

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: Rebuked Rabbi Yirmeya with a verse from Proverbs.

terms.meaning: Tefillin: leather boxes holding Torah passages, worn on arm and head during prayer and study.

18.note: Rav Ashi made a wedding feast for his son and saw that the Sages were very merry. He brought a cup of white glass, broke it in front of them, and they became sad.
18.why: It follows Mar son of Ravina breaking a cup worth four hundred zuz at his son's wedding, in a run of stories showing that even in rejoicing there should be trembling.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: Broke a white glass cup at his son's wedding to sober the guests.

19.note: At the wedding feast of Mar son of Ravina, the Sages asked Rav Hamnuna Zuti to sing for them. He sang: Woe to us, for we shall die; woe to us, for we shall die. They asked what refrain they should answer, and he told them: Where is Torah and where is mitzva, that protect us?
19.why: It belongs to a run of wedding stories about curbing excessive joy, and is followed by Rabbi Yoḥanan's teaching in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai that one may not fill one's mouth with laughter in this world.

people.name: Rav Hamnuna Zuti
people.about: Asked to sing at a wedding; sang of death instead.

people.name: Mar son of Ravina
people.about: Host of the wedding feast.

terms.meaning: A commandment, or a good deed done in fulfillment of one.

20.note: Rav Kahana accompanied Rav Shimi bar Ashi from Pum Nahara to the palm grove of Babylonia. When they arrived, Rav Kahana asked what people mean when they say these palms have been there since Adam. Rav Shimi bar Ashi said he had been reminded of a teaching of Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Ḥanina on Jeremiah's land where no man passed and no person settled: every land Adam decreed would be settled was settled, and every land he decreed would not be settled was not.
20.why: A teaching had just said one should part from another with a matter of Torah, so that he will remember him; this parting, which ends in a new teaching, is given as an example.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: Accompanied Rav Shimi bar Ashi and asked about the palms.

people.name: Rav Shimi bar Ashi
people.about: Answered with a teaching of Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Ḥanina.

terms.meaning: The first human, Adam; the Hebrew word for person in the verse is also adam.
